archetype.name: Retooling (run-first, pass-broken)
archetype.definition: A team a year removed from a top-10 offense whose passing game and ball security have collapsed, leaving a functional run game and a middling defense with nothing to carry them.

report.headline: A real run game buried under the league's worst passing attack and turnovers
report.take:
The Colts are 3-8, and the record is roughly what they are. The underlying numbers are only a shade kinder. Their point differential implies 4.8 wins, and Wins Over Expected sits at -1.79 thanks to a 0.2 one-score win rate, so a couple of coin flips have gone against them. But net EPA ranks 29th, and that is not a team close to good. The more striking context is history. Last season this offense ranked 7th in EPA and scored 27.4 points a game. This year it ranks 31st, with Daniel Jones starting every game, so this is not a quarterback-carousel story. The passing game itself has stopped working.

The split inside the offense is stark. On the ground the Colts are a good team: rush EPA ranks 9th, run success 7th, and the line's run EPA 6th, with Jonathan Taylor taking the overwhelming share of carries. Through the air they are the worst in football, with pass EPA of -0.187, dead last. The game log shows passing EPA in the red almost every week, bottoming out at -17.6 in the 42-7 loss at Jacksonville. Layer on 20 turnovers and a -12 turnover differential, 31st per game, and you have an offense that moves the ball on the ground and then hands it back.

The defense is mediocre rather than broken, and some of its numbers mislead in both directions. It is good at getting off the field: third-down conversions allowed rank 5th and success rate allowed 13th. It also allows big plays, ranking 29th in explosive pass rate allowed and 28th on explosive runs. It barely pressures the quarterback (27th) and has taken the ball away only six times by the EPA feed, 31st. Opposing lead backs have feasted, with the Colts ranking last against RB1s by both EPA and PPR over average. Points allowed of 27.7 a game, 30th, overstate the defense somewhat, because the turnover pile keeps handing opponents short fields.

Where it goes from here depends on bodies as much as schemes. Both starting tackles (Jalen Travis, Bernhard Raimann) and both starting corners (Charvarius Ward, Sauce Gardner) are out for the Giants game, and the backup back Seth McGowan is out until mid-December. Quiet strengths like special teams (6th in EPA per game), discipline (3rd-fewest penalties) and time of possession (8th) keep games closer than the talent gap suggests. Still, this roster is playing out the string unless the passing game finds even a pulse.

strengths.title: The run game genuinely works
strengths.body: Rushing is the one phase where the Colts are above average: rush EPA ranks 9th and the line's run success rate 7th, with Taylor carrying the bulk of the load. It isn't a product of positive game script, since they have trailed often. That makes it a real line-and-back strength. The risk is that both starting tackles are out, and the Houston game (38 rushing yards) showed how quickly it can dry up.

strengths.title: Wins the hidden-yardage battles
strengths.body: Special teams rank 6th in EPA per game, the team commits the 3rd-fewest penalties, and it ranks 8th in time of possession. That combination comes from a run-leaning, disciplined operation, and it is the reason several losses stayed within a score. It should hold, because it doesn't depend on the passing game.

strengths.title: Third-down defense gets off the field
strengths.body: Opponents convert only 32.4% of third downs, 5th-best, and the defense's down-to-down success rate allowed is a respectable 13th. That is a sign of sound structure, even though the unit gives up chunk plays. With both starting corners out, sustaining it on third-and-long gets much harder in the short term.

concerns.title: The passing game has collapsed
concerns.body: Pass EPA is last in the league, a steep fall for an offense that ranked 7th in EPA last season. Protection is part of it, with QB hit rate allowed 28th, but the bigger problem is the volume of negative plays and interceptions. With both starting tackles now out, there is little reason to expect a quick fix.

concerns.title: Turnovers are deciding games
concerns.body: Twenty giveaways against eight takeaways produce a -12 differential, and the Colts have lost the turnover battle in almost every game. Some of that regresses, especially the defense's low takeaway count. The giveaways, though, are tied to a struggling pass offense and are more likely to persist.

concerns.title: No rush, and big plays allowed
concerns.body: Pressure rate ranks 27th, and the defense allows the 29th-ranked explosive pass rate and the 28th-ranked explosive rush rate. Lead backs have run wild against it, ranking last by EPA allowed to RB1s. Without its top two corners, the coverage that has masked the weak rush is thinner than ever.

trend.note: Early-season games at Kansas City and Washington showed a competitive team, but since late October the passing EPA has been deeply negative almost every week. The last trip out ended 26-3 at Houston with just 38 rushing yards.

nextGame.headline: Shorthanded Colts need Taylor and clean hands against fortunate Giants
nextGame.body:
The Book has the Giants by 6.5 with a 41.5 total, and the Colts at +260 on the moneyline. New York's 6-3-1 record runs well ahead of its play: Wins Over Expected ranks 2nd and point differential only 15th. Still, the Giants are a sound defense, 5th in yards allowed per game and 2nd in deep-ball EPA allowed, and that clamps down on tight ends, a problem when Tyler Warren is the Colts' most-targeted player. Their weaknesses are the league's lowest pressure rate and the worst red-zone touchdown rate allowed. On offense they run more than the situation suggests despite a 24th-ranked rush EPA, and they pass to tight ends more than the league does.

Availability tilts against Indianapolis. Both starting tackles, Travis and Raimann, are out, and so are both starting corners, Ward and Gardner. Tillery, Mallory and McGowan are also out, which puts nearly all the backfield work on Taylor, and Alec Pierce remains on injured reserve. New York is missing corner Greg Newsome for multiple weeks. The Giants have cycled through three quarterbacks, with J.J. McCarthy starting the last four. The Colts at least come in on 10 days of rest after their Thursday game.

waysToWin.title: Ride Taylor and own the clock
waysToWin.body: The Colts' run game is their one top-10 unit, and the Giants' run defense is merely solid. A steady diet of Taylor keeps Jones out of obvious passing downs and shortens a low-total game. The Colts have already won time of possession most weeks.

waysToWin.title: Cash in inside the 20
waysToWin.body: The Giants allow red-zone touchdowns at the league's worst rate. They also bring the least pressure in football, which softens the blow of two backup tackles. If the Colts can string together a few long drives, the scores should come as touchdowns rather than field goals.

waysToWin.title: Make McCarthy beat them
waysToWin.body: New York's offense leans on a run game that ranks 24th in EPA, behind a line that allows a high sack rate. If the Colts' 5th-ranked third-down defense forces long conversions, the Giants' luck-inflated close-game magic could run out.

waysToLose.title: Giveaways hand over short fields
waysToLose.body: The Colts have turned it over at a rate only one team matches, and the Giants are an average takeaway team. In a game projected in the low 40s, two giveaways could be the whole margin.

waysToLose.title: Depleted secondary meets Giant tight ends
waysToLose.body: With Ward and Gardner out, a defense already 28th against opposing TE1s and 31st against WR3s has to cover a Giants offense that funnels extra targets to tight ends. That is where McCarthy will find easy completions.

waysToLose.title: Passing game has nowhere to go
waysToLose.body: The Giants take away the two things the Colts' passing game wants: they allow the 2nd-lowest EPA on deep balls and hold TE1s well under their averages. If Taylor is bottled up, the league's worst passing offense is left facing a matchup that suits it poorly.

nextGame.watch: How the two backup tackles handle the Giants' front on early downs. If Taylor can still find yards before contact, the Colts can keep this a one-score game.

restOfSeason.body:
After the Giants the schedule splits in two. Road trips to Philadelphia (29th-ranked offense) and Tennessee (30th-ranked defense) are real chances to add wins. Home games against Cincinnati's 2nd-ranked offense and Jacksonville's 2nd-ranked defense, plus a trip to Cleveland, look like losses for this roster. Some regression in the Colts' favor is fair to expect: the one-score record and the takeaway drought are partly bad luck, and the differential says they've been a bit better than 3-8.

The core problem won't regress away. A last-ranked passing offense that keeps turning the ball over caps the scoring, and the injuries at tackle and corner make the next few weeks worse before anyone returns. Expect a run-heavy team that keeps games respectable against weak opponents and gets separated by good ones.
swingFactors: Returns of Travis, Raimann, Ward and Gardner

confidence.note: Eleven games with one starting QB is a solid read, but heavy injuries at tackle and corner cloud the near term.
